en: I bow to you, the Lord Viṣṇu, the cause of the existence of all things, who is to be meditated upon within the heart by those possessing knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātma-jñāna).
Free from the dualities of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, it is the supreme One, pure existence alone, dwelling in the hearts of all, whose form is pure consciousness. || 1 ||

Having restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths within the heart through resolute intellect, and having severed all bonds of doubt and the floods of sense-objects, the ascetics—freed from delusion—behold that Lord Rāma, who wears a jewel-crested crown and shines like the sun; him I worship.

I bow to Rāma, who transcends illusion, the primordial Mādhava, the source of the universe, beyond all measure, the destroyer of delusion, and the one worshipped by sages; he who is the object of meditation for yogis, the very method of yoga, the perfectly complete, who delights the world, and is most beautiful. 3.

I bow to Rāma, the fire that consumes all demons, who is free from the notions of existence and non-existence, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by those foremost in worldly existence yet attached to enjoyments, and who is eternal, pure, awakened, infinite, and known as the syllable Om (Praṇava). 4.
You are my protector, the performer of every task for which you are entreated; you are beyond pride, the form of Mādhava, and the sustainer of all.
You are accessible through devotion, the one whose form is meditated upon, the remover of worldly existence, and the companion to those whose minds are purified by the practice of yoga.

I bow to Rāma, the beautiful one, dark as a blue lotus, the beginningless and endless supreme Lord of the multitudes of worlds; he who is not to be attained by worldly measures, but is to be worshipped by those endowed with devotion, faith, and a sincere disposition.

Who indeed is capable of knowing you—Mādhava, who have transcended pride yet are free from ego, who are attached to honor, who are honored by sages, who are saluted by hosts of gods in the forest of Vṛndāvana, who are worshipped by the faces of the Bhavas (Śivas), and who are the root of happiness? I bow to Rāma.

I bow to Rāma, the Lord of Mathurā, who is emerald-green in hue; he is the eternal bliss and objectless knowledge to be established by various scriptures and the collection of Vedas, who is without beginning, and who has assumed a human form for the sake of serving me.

That mortal on earth who, endowed with faith, recites this primordial hymn to Brahmā—the ordinance for the knowledge of Brahman—and meditates upon the dark-hued Rāma, the Lord who grants all desired objects, shall become a meditator freed from the multitudes of sins. (9)
Thus ends the hymn to Rāma composed by Brahmā and the gods, in the Yuddhakāṇḍa of the glorious Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa.
